body: Ref: https://forum.syncthing.net/t/syncthing-2-0-migration-running-for-27-hours-and-counting/24788

I had the same problem as pointed out in forum, two nodes syncing using syncthing:
62,122 files 24,678 directories ~13.8 TiB
One of nodes migrated to v2 in less than an hour.
The other one seems to freeze after a couple of hours.

Two nodes are identical in cpu, memory, disks, operating system and everything.

It got a little faster with `ignorePerms` true. And right now 60000 file scanning is in 70% after 24 hours.

It took four days, but it has done it. In the end all folders just displayed the Unknown state. I could not do anything. Settings, logs, nothing worked in the GUI. Maybe my config.xml was not fully compatible with 2.x. Deleted everything and now it does the indexing again.

body: I think this less about the number of files (although you could run into that as well) and more about the number of blocks, as that tends to be one or two magnitudes higher.

Maybe we can apply some sharding here? The same technique helped us scaling at the folder level. But I fear it's going to be a lot harder as we ultimately need transactional behaviour which won't work across multiple sqlite databases...

Yeah that's what I'm thinking, it's a bit tricky as there are keys towards blocklists and stuff as well, and also we'd need to do this a bit dynamically as it will be a lot of overhead to do sharding for small folders.

Also trying to come up with potential tradeoffs where we don't store all the block hashes but some sort of partial hint, so that we can shift some work towards when we need to do the block lookup, but nothing obvious comes to mind so far (that would significantly reduce the number of rows to something below the number of blocks in total).

(The use for this data is when syncing a change, we want to see if we already have a given block locally somewhere in order to avoid downloading it again, and that lookup is by block hash.)

(https://github.com/syncthing/syncthing/blob/main/internal/db/sqlite/sql/schema/folder/50-blocks.sql for the record)

The blocklists table is the main offender judging from real world stats:

https://forum.syncthing.net/t/database-or-disk-is-full-might-be-syncthing-might-be-qnap/24930/7

That's ~85% of the whole DB layer

In terms of size on disk, yes, but the blocks table is going to have orders of magnitude more rows (and hence inserts-per-file). I guess a benchmark is required to determine which is which in terms of taking a long time to insert.

I tested by simplifying the benchmark to just inserts, increasing the blocks per file to 1000 to simulate large files, and then commenting out either the blocklist insert or the block insert (https://github.com/syncthing/syncthing/compare/main...calmh:syncthing:benchmarkinserts?expand=1).

Skipping just block lists still has it slow enough that I don't even have the patience to wait for the next benchmark level:


So it's rather a thing influenced by row count and in turn index updates? Maybe we can partition the blocks table as a startpoint.
(I deleted a hopeful but incorrect comment.)
Using multiple block tables seemed to make things worse for me.
We could try to avoid a lot of index shuffling if we insert the blocks in order aka sorting them according to the PK prior to inserting them.

There is no relevant sort order when it's indexed on hash which is essentially random and we're inserting random records in a table with many millions of rows already. I tried switching the primary key ordering but there are other complications, PR coming shortly with a couple of improvements...

issue.title: refactor(db): slightly improve insert performance
issue.body: This just removes an unnecessary foreign key constraint, where we already do the garbage collection manually in the database service. However, as part of getting here I tried a couple of other variants along the way: - Changing the order of the primary key from `(hash, blocklist_hash, idx)` to `(blocklist_hash, idx, hash)` so that inserts would be naturally ordered. However this requires a new index `on blocks (hash)` so that we can still look up blocks by hash, and turns out to be strictly worse than what we already have. - Removing the primary key entirely and the `WITHOUT ROWID` to make it a rowid table without any required order, and an index as above. This is faster when the table is small, but becomes slower when it's large (due to dual indexes I guess). These are the benchmark results from current `main`, the second alternative below ("Index(hash)") and this proposal that retains the combined primary key ("combined"). Overall it ends up being about 65% faster. Ref #10264

body:
I have some changes that might be relevant, though I didn't deem them worthy of PRing yet. Anyway, this is the most efficient variant of my changes based on my benchmark results, but it's also likely overdone. However the batching of blocks within a transaction imo makes sense regardless of how we insert after (this also uses prepared statements for various possible sizes, to minimize DB calls - that's possibly/likely not so impactful, need to check still):

https://github.com/syncthing/syncthing/compare/main...imsodin:syncthing:db-batch-grouped-all_prepared

Also seems like the issues are mainly with migration and initial sync, at least I feel like that's the pattern from reports so far where typically people seem to be fine once the found a way to get over the initial inserts (migration or rescan). And as we constantly write, the DB maybe can't optimize during that time - maybe there's something to be done manually on very large/long-lasting continuous inserts?

> There is no relevant sort order when it's indexed on hash which is essentially random and we're inserting random records in a table with many millions of rows already.

The order might make a difference. See section `Index key value randomness` of https://voidstar.tech/sqlite_insert_speed/

Our usage pattern would equate to the "Shuffled" test case. This would result in a 20x slowdown compared to sequential inserts, assuming these figures are accurate.

Yeah, if you're going to insert a million rows in an empty table, better do it in order. No argument from me, and that's what they're testing. However, when you have a table with ten million random rows in it, the order in which you insert the next thousand random rows has no practical significance -- they're going to be in a thousand different random pages regardless. I've just benchmarked it. Prove me wrong.

Or, put another way, during migration only, it would be nice to process blocks in order. We can't do that because we're dealing with files and get the blocks they have in the order they have them. We can sort each individual block list, _but it doesn't matter_.

I think there's two or three different parts to this issue:

- We should find a better way to scale the large block table. We're not there yet, though it's faster now than it was on launch day.
- The migration process is giving slightly misleading output, as files/s is usually not the limiting factor but blocks/s. With the numbers from the initial issue description, we have `30028318 / (23*3600 + 24*60) ~= 350` blocks/s insertion rate happening. That's not blazingly fast, but it's moving. However, ...
- ... on my laptop, currently (at approximately the same point as the OP, 61k files, 30M blocks): `db_bench_test.go:72: t=11m2.694011084s, files=61700, blocks=30850000, files/s=93.1, blocks/s=46552.4` (average up to that point; instant rate was about half)

So I'm not really sure what's going on with the OP. Really slow storage? But it doesn't seem absolutely inherent to the code.
